SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Saturday that his presidential term would end in 2030 and that the question of his departure from office was settled, reaffirming that Egypt's constitution would not be amended. "I said that the Egyptian constitution would not be touched," he said. "This is an entirely settled matter and will not be discussed," he added, referring to the end of his current term. Sisi, 71, is serving a six-year term after winning re-election in December 2023. Constitutional amendments approved in a 2019 referendum extended presidential terms to six years from four and allowed Sisi to seek a third term, clearing the way for him to remain in office until 2030. A former general, Sisi rose to power in 2013 by toppling Egypt's first democratically elected president, Mohamed Mursi, after mass protests against his rule. He made the remarks on Saturday while attending a graduation ceremony for new classes at the Egyptian Military Academy.

item.title: Rising household costs undermine economic mobility, push Americans to delay major life decisions: McKinsey
item.description: Rising living costs are the biggest barrier to economic mobility for 60 per cent of Americans, while nine out of ten say food and grocery expenses are putting pressure on their household finances, ...
item.content:encoded:
Rising household costs undermine economic mobility, push Americans to delay major life decisions: McKinsey Rising living costs are the biggest barrier to economic mobility for 60 per cent of Americans, while nine out of ten say food and grocery expenses are putting pressure on their household finances, according to a report by the McKinsey Institute for Economic Mobility. ANI | Updated: 17-10-2026 13:50 IST | Created: 17-10-2026 13:50 IST

Representative Image (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Rising living costs are the biggest barrier to economic mobility for 60 per cent of Americans, while nine out of ten say food and grocery expenses are putting pressure on their household finances, according to a report by the McKinsey Institute for Economic Mobility. The report said affordability pressures are affecting people's ability to plan for the future, pursue education, change jobs and make long-term investments, potentially limiting their chances of improving their economic position. The research, based on a survey of 30,000 Americans, found that two-thirds identified greater financial security as their top aspiration, regardless of race, income or where they live. “By far, the rising cost of living was the number one thing people cited—60 percent of Americans said that’s the thing getting in the way of them achieving their dreams,” JP Julien, a partner at McKinsey, said in the report. Food and groceries emerged as the most widely reported source of household financial pressure, ranking ahead of housing, fuel, healthcare and education costs. The report also highlighted differences across life stages. Young adults were more focused on careers and income and were more likely than other respondents to identify mental health as a barrier to progress. Parents were particularly concerned about the cost of living and opportunities for their children, while people approaching retirement prioritised saving for the future. The report also found that community connections were linked to a greater sense of control over one's future. People who felt strongly connected to their communities were twice as likely to say they had a say in the direction of their lives and three times as likely to feel in control of their future. “The reality is that affordability pressures change how people imagine their future,” Diana Ellsworth, a senior partner at McKinsey, said, adding that rising costs can make people hesitant to change jobs, pursue education or make other long-term investments. The report called for action to make essential expenses, including housing, food and childcare, more affordable, while ensuring families have sufficient income. It also stressed the need for more reliable pathways into good jobs and opportunities for career progression. McKinsey said employers, educators and policymakers could support economic mobility through skills-based hiring, paid training, apprenticeships, flexible work arrangements and stronger community institutions. (ANI)

item.title: US waives Russian-oil tariffs, but uncertainty prevails as Washington retains leverage: GTRI
item.description: The United States' decision to waive additional tariffs linked to India's purchases of Russian oil provides temporary relief to New Delhi but offers no lasting certainty, as Washington retains the ...
item.content:encoded:
US waives Russian-oil tariffs, but uncertainty prevails as Washington retains leverage: GTRI The United States' decision to waive additional tariffs linked to India's purchases of Russian oil provides temporary relief to New Delhi but offers no lasting certainty, as Washington retains the authority to reinstate the duties, according to a report by the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI). ANI | Updated: 17-10-2026 13:24 IST | Created: 17-10-2026 13:24 IST

Representative Image (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

The United States' decision to waive additional tariffs linked to India's purchases of Russian oil provides temporary relief to New Delhi but offers no lasting certainty, as Washington retains the authority to reinstate the duties, according to a report by the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI). US President Donald Trump waived the punitive tariffs on October 16 under the newly enacted Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 (SRIA), easing the threat of additional duties of up to 100 per cent on goods from major buyers of Russian oil. However, the report noted that the underlying legislation remains in force, allowing Washington to withdraw the waiver at any time and use the threat of tariffs as leverage in future bilateral trade negotiations. "The waiver has no fixed expiry date, but it can be withdrawn," GTRI said in its report, highlighting the uncertainty surrounding India's trade and energy security outlook. The US Trade Representative will continue monitoring Russian energy purchases, enabling the administration to review the waiver and potentially revive the additional duties, the report added. GTRI identified several factors that may have influenced Washington's decision to suspend the penalties, including its own energy requirements, the tariff arrangement with China and the potential impact on ongoing trade negotiations with India. Under an October 9 agreement with Russia, the US decided to purchase Russian diesel to address domestic shortages and high fuel prices. Penalising other countries for buying Russian energy while making similar purchases itself could expose Washington to accusations of double standards, the report observed. The report also highlighted Washington's agreement not to increase tariffs on China until January 10, following a deal reached during Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the US last month. Targeting India with additional duties while China remains protected could complicate ongoing bilateral trade negotiations, it added. For India, the waiver provides breathing room but does not eliminate the risk of renewed trade pressure. According to GTRI, Russia's share of India's oil imports declined from 51 per cent in July to 44 per cent in August as New Delhi increased purchases from the US and the United Arab Emirates. Despite this shift, the continued validity of SRIA leaves Washington free to revive the tariff threat and potentially seek further concessions from India in bilateral trade talks. GTRI cautioned that India should prioritise energy security, purchase oil on commercial terms and prepare for the possibility of renewed US pressure. The report notes that India should treat the decision as temporary relief rather than a durable resolution of the underlying trade dispute. (ANI)

item.title: US State Department report keeps China in Tier 3 over forced labour, trafficking concerns
item.description: China has remained in Tier 3 in the United States State Department's 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report, with the assessment citing widespread forced labour concerns, arbitrary detention of ethnic and ...
item.content:encoded:
US State Department report keeps China in Tier 3 over forced labour, trafficking concerns China has remained in Tier 3 in the United States State Department's 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report, with the assessment citing widespread forced labour concerns, arbitrary detention of ethnic and religious minorities, and insufficient efforts to combat human trafficking. ANI | Updated: 17-10-2026 12:33 IST | Created: 17-10-2026 12:33 IST

Representative Image (Image Source: Reuters) . Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

China has remained in Tier 3 category in the United States State Department’s 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report, with the assessment citing widespread forced labour concerns, arbitrary detention of ethnic and religious minorities, and insufficient efforts to combat human trafficking. The report said the Chinese government did not fully meet the minimum standards for eliminating trafficking and was not making significant efforts to do so. It highlighted alleged forced labour in government-affiliated sectors, particularly in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, where Uyghurs, ethnic Kazakhs, ethnic Kyrgyz and members of other minority groups continued to face arbitrary detention under the stated objectives of “vocational training” and “deradicalisation”. According to the report, authorities also continued to place ethnic Tibetans, Uyghurs and other minority groups in vocational training and manufacturing jobs through purported poverty alleviation and labour dispatch programmes that featured coercive elements. The assessment further alleged that forced labour practices extended to other Chinese provinces and that authorities sought to coerce the repatriation and internment of ethnic and religious minorities living abroad, increasing their vulnerability to exploitation. The report also accused Chinese officials of knowingly permitting North Korean citizens to be subjected to forced labour in China. It raised concerns over inadequate oversight of recruitment channels, contracts and working conditions for Chinese nationals employed on Belt and Road Initiative projects and other China-linked infrastructure projects overseas. On law enforcement, the report said China had failed to provide complete trafficking-related data for the ninth consecutive year and had not reported identifying any trafficking victims or referring them to protection services during the reporting period. Although Chinese authorities reportedly investigated and prosecuted some crimes that may have amounted to human trafficking, the report assessed overall enforcement efforts as insufficient. It also noted that cases involving indicators of forced labour were frequently handled as administrative matters rather than prosecuted under anti-trafficking laws. The report outlined gaps in China’s legal framework, including provisions addressing the abduction and sale of women and children that do not explicitly require exploitation as an element of the offence. Tier 3 is the lowest ranking in the State Department’s trafficking assessment, reserved for governments that do not fully meet minimum standards and are not making significant efforts to comply. (ANI)
